use_case: TaraHome blog cover for a homeowner guide to fixing an unreliable Zigbee network
prompt: Use case and style: photorealistic-natural editorial blog cover for TaraHome, landscape 3:2. Story: a calm, practical homeowner is fixing an unreliable Zigbee smart-home network in a warm, lived-in living room. Show one continuous real residential scene: a person's hand repositioning a small generic unbranded Zigbee coordinator or radio dongle on a normal USB extension cable, moving it away from a compact home-automation computer and an ordinary Wi-Fi router on an open oak console. In the room, include subtle evidence of the devices being protected by the mesh: one lit floor lamp and one small unbranded door or contact sensor, both realistically installed and secondary to the scene. The setup should feel plausible, safe, tidy, and easy for a homeowner to understand. TaraHome direction: warm late-morning natural window light, plaster wall, oak and linen materials, soft off-white and warm neutral palette, restrained dark forest-green accents in a cushion or small ceramic object, calm premium editorial photography, believable device scale and cable routing, gentle depth of field, modest lived-in texture rather than a showroom. Composition: wide horizontal 3:2 frame, eye-level three-quarter angle, open breathing room, the hand and USB extension action near the center, compact computer and router separated visibly but naturally, lamp and sensor readable in the wider room; keep important subjects within a wide center-safe area for 16:9 and 16:10 center crops. No close-up product glamour shot and no named commercial model. Hard exclusions: no words, letters, numbers, logos, brand marks, headline, title poster, captions, labels, screens, dashboards, smartphone UI, fake interface, icons, Wi-Fi symbol, Zigbee symbol, arrows, decorative routing or network lines, dotted paths, topology map, chart, graph, infographic, translucent panel, inset frame, floating UI card, progress bar, sci-fi glow, neon, beige device diagram, duplicated devices, impossible ports, impossible cables, floating hardware, server-rack aesthetic, excessive greenery, clutter, or visible safety hazard. Do not imitate or invent a specific branded product; use only generic, unbranded standard device categories as environmental props.
